config.text:
﻿What is the Water ICAT?

The Water Infrastructure and Capacity Assessment Tool (ICAT) is a mapping tool used to screen for drinking water systems and wastewater facilities with potential water infrastructure needs. Within the context of this tool, "need" refers to utilities that are potentially experiencing water infrastructure and technical, managerial, or financial capacity challenges.

functionConfig.altText: Map widgets including showing the map filter, layer, legend, and add data icons.

config.text:
Map Functionalities


This tool is interactive and contains widgets that allow the user to perform various functions.


  • Select: Use this widget to select and to filter for water utilities within a drawn geographic boundary. This widget can help users wanting to limit screening results to those within a specified area. This widget can be used before applying map filters or after applying map filters, depending on screening goals.  


  • Filter the map: Use this widget to filter for utilities that meet desired screening criteria.


  • Turn on/off map layers: Use this widget to turn on or turn off map layers.


  • View map legend: Use this widget to view and understand map "symbology", or what the colors/symbols used in the map represent. The legend only populates for map layers currently turned on.


  • Add your own data/map layers: This widget allows the user to add custom data/map layers to their CURRENT session; data/maps added to a session DO NOT save for future sessions. After selecting the data to add to the map, be sure to select, "Add to Map", as shown in the figure on the right.


  • Change map basemap: This widget allows the user to change the map basemap. Options include streets, aerial imagery, and topographic basemaps, among others.


  • Print/export map image: This widget allows the user to print an image of the map, including the map legend, title, and other configurable layout options.

How to Reset Filters


To reset map filters, use the "reset button" located on the bottom right corner of each filter category.


Each filter category (e.g., “General”, “Demographic”, “Compliance”, etc.) has its own reset button as shown on the figure. If filters are applied under more than one category, this step must be done for EACH category.

config.text:
Exporting Data


There are two ways to export data - through the map page OR through the data table page. Learn more below.

Drinking Water Data Field Descriptions


Visit Source Data to learn more about the data sources listed and data refresh intervals.


4-Log Treatment or Greater (Y/N)

4-log treatment of groundwater is a treatment technique that removes or inactivates 99.99% of viruses in source groundwater. Systems using greater than 4-log treatment remove or inactivate more than 99.99% of viruses from source groundwater.


Data Source: SDWIS (Safe Drinking Water Information System) Fed Reporting System


Additional Enforcement/Compliance Details

Provides link to the water system's Enforcement and Compliance History Online (ECHO) Detailed Facility Report (DFR).


The DFR presents a concise enforcement and compliance history for a selected facility. Additional information can be found here: https://echo.epa.gov/help/reports/detailed-facility-report-help


Data Source: Enforcement and Compliance History Online (ECHO) Data Downloads


Bureau of Indian Affairs Tribe Code

Three digit code identifying the Tribal Government, assigned by the Bureau of Indian Affairs.


Data Source: SDWIS (Safe Drinking Water Information System) Fed Reporting System


City(ies) Served

Indicates the name of the city(ies) the system serves.


Data Source: SDWIS (Safe Drinking Water Information System) Fed Reporting System


County(ies) Served

Indicates the name of the county(ies) the system serves.


Data Source: SDWIS (Safe Drinking Water Information System) Fed Reporting System


Data Verification Sanitary Survey Element Results (Most Recent Complete Survey)

Data verification is one of the eight elements/areas of the sanitary survey. This survey element determines water system conformance with regulatory requirements through the review of water quality monitoring plans and system records; verifies data reported to the regulatory agency are consistent with system records.


Possible survey outcomes include:

  1. Minor deficiencies
  2. No deficiencies or recommendations
  3. Recommendations made
  4. Significant deficiencies
  5. Not evaluated
  6. Not applicable

If the action level for lead is exceeded, the system must also inform the public about steps they should take to protect their health and may have to replace lead service lines under their control.

Data Table Overview


What utilities populate in the data table?

The map and data tables are dynamically linked. This means that the data table reflects all map filters a user has currently applied.


Conversely, if additional filters selections are made using table filter functionalities, the map will reflect these changes.


﻿Example: The wastewater map was filtered for all systems in Region 1. This populates 436 wastewater facilities. When navigating to the Data Tables and Export page, only those filtered facilities display in the table. This is indicated by the "Total: 436" seen on the data table page. This value matches the total count of facilities shown on the map page.


Important note for drinking water tables

Because there are two tables for drinking water systems - a table for systems with spatial data and a table for systems without spatial data - users must repeat filter selections made within the table view, across both tables. If this step is not taken, when viewing the map, only one layer will show the additional filter selections made (the layer for which additional filters were selected within the table view).

Tool Design


This section describes how the Water ICAT enables users to screen for potential need.


What does “need” mean within the context of the Water ICAT and what does this mean for users of the Water ICAT?

Need can be defined in several ways given the context in which it is used. Within Water ICAT, need is conceptualized broadly as the result of an infrastructure challenge and/or a technical, managerial, or financial capacity challenge.

 

For users of the Water ICAT, it can be helpful to keep this conceptual framework (as well as the user’s specific screening goals) in mind when making screening selections from available data filters.

 

Does the Water ICAT create a single index value for need?

No, the Water ICAT does not create a single index value of need for each utility. Instead, the Water ICAT includes data filters organized by data type (such as, compliance related data; community characteristic data; infrastructure funding data, etc.) that a user can select from based on their screening goals.


What categories of data are included within the Water ICAT?

The Water ICAT includes three primary types of data: (1) enforcement/compliance (violation) data, (2) infrastructure funding data, and (3) environmental justice/disadvantaged community data.

 

  1. Enforcement/compliance (violation) data are included because, although this data may be lagging indicators of a problem, it can help users identify utilities that are having ongoing or more significant compliance challenges. Root cause(s) of a given violation will be unique to each utility and could be due to capacity (technical, managerial, financial) related factors, such as, staffing challenges, difficulty keeping up with regulatory changes, infrastructure related factors (including inadequate maintenance), or aging infrastructure. While it not possible to discern a specific root cause with enforcement/compliance data alone, these data can provide users a starting point for identifying utilities that are having challenges significant enough to result in noncompliance.
  2. State Revolving Fund (SRF) Infrastructure funding data are included to enable users to know if a utility has received SRF water infrastructure funding in the past. Past receipt of water infrastructure funding can provide insight into a utility’s capacity to successfully identify, apply for, and receive funding. Additionally, some assistance providers may wish to prioritize utilities that have not received funding from a particular source in the past. While it can be helpful to have this information, there are other sources of SRF water infrastructure funding that utilities may use beyond what is incorporated within the Water ICAT.
  3. Environmental Justice/Disadvantaged Community data are included when adequate spatial data are available to know the actual or approximated service area for a utility. These data provide insight into the population that comprises a utility’s (actual or approximated) service area. Utilities serving populations that are majority disadvantaged or with potential environmental justice concerns may face unique and compounding challenges. Such utilities may have capacity and resource limitations or may have experienced historical underinvestment.

 

Each of these data types have their own caveats and limitations; visit Caveats and Limitations for information.

 ____

Figure Right: This figure depicts the conceptual design and primary data used within the Water ICAT. When a utility has an infrastructure challenge and potential technical, managerial, or financial (TMF) capacity challenges, the utility may have assistance needs. The primary data incorporated into the Water ICAT are enforcement/compliance data, water infrastructure funding data, and environmental justice/disadvantaged community data.

﻿Appropriate Use


While data are powerful aids in identifying where potential water infrastructure needs may exist across states, tribes, and territories – this tool should be used for screening purposes for potential technical assistance versus a definitive indication of need.


As discussed on the Tool Design and Caveats and Limitations pages, Water ICAT uses indicators of need as opposed to direct measures. Because of these limitations, Water ICAT should only be used for screening.

 

What is an example of appropriate use as a screening tool?

Outreach for technical assistance could be a common use of Water ICAT. In this use scenario,


  1. Users select their screening requirements using the available map filters to identify utilities with potential assistance needs. The result is a list of utilities with potential needs.
  2. Users then "ground-truth" and gain additional context about the utilities identified (such as, more detailed information about their specific needs, challenges, and communities served). One way this can be done is by speaking with the EPA Region OR the state/tribe/territory where the utility is located. This can result in helpful context, for example, a utility may already be receiving help from another entity OR the facility may have just received funding to address its infrastructure need. The result of this “ground-truthing” is a further refined list of communities that may require assistance.
  3. After getting additional context on the screening list, users can reach out to the refined list of utilities to begin the discussion on helping the community access beneficial resources.

 

What is an example of inappropriate use? An example of inappropriate use would be any application that characterizes the screening list of utilities as having definitive needs, WITHOUT having first consulted additional information and/or local knowledge.

 

Note: To learn about EPA assistance resources, visit the Assistance Resources page.


_______

Figure: This graphic depicts the intended use of Water ICAT - screen for water utilities with potential needs, ground truth the data with local context, then connect utilities with beneficial resources.

Infrastructure Types


Water ICAT includes water infrastructure types where there are high quality, nationally comprehensive data. Currently, these types include:


  1. Drinking Water: Community Water Systems (CWS) and
  2. Wastewater: National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permitted Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTWs).


The limiting factor in not including other infrastructure types (such as, stormwater systems**, private domestic wells, septic systems, and non-discharging wastewater facilities) is national data availability. As data availability improves, more water infrastructure types may be added to this tool.

 

NOTE: EPA is undergoing efforts to improve the accuracy of the wastewater data. As such, Water ICAT may include a few municipal separate storm sewer systems (MS4s) but does not contain a comprehensive dataset, so the tool should not be used to screen for potential water infrastructure needs at MS4 facilities.


______

Photo credit: Florida Water Daily

Connecting Communities with Resources


Some users of Water ICAT may be able to provide assistance themselves (e.g., may be a technical assistance provider). Other users may not be an assistance provider, but instead an entity that works to connect communities with assistance providers. For the latter, EPA has a water infrastructure technical assistance program called WaterTA. Through EPA's WaterTA program, communities can receive assistance on activities ranging lead service line inventories, capacity development support, compliance assistance, funding applications, and more. Below are helpful links to learn more about EPA's WaterTA program:


  1. About EPA's WaterTA program: https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure/water-technical-assistance-waterta
  2. List of WaterTA programs: https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure/water-technical-assistance-programs
  3. WaterTA Request Form (submit a request for TA): https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure/forms/water-technical-assistance-request-form


Additionally, states often have their own water infrastructure technical assistance programs as well as other federal agencies such as USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture), HUD (Housing and Urban Development), and IHS (Indian Health Service).


Finally, the USEPA maintains Water Finance Clearinghouse, a web‐based portal that can help communities locate information and resources to inform on decisions about drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater infrastructure needs: https://www.epa.gov/waterfinancecenter/water-finance-clearinghouse-portal.

Key Terms


Community Water System (CWS)

A type of public water system that supplies water to the same population year-round.

 

Facility

A term used interchangeably with “Publicly Owned Treatment Works” or “wastewater facility.”

 

National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Permitted Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTW)

A POTW is a treatment plant owned by a State or municipality and is designed to provide treatment (including recycling and reclamation) of municipal sewage and industrial waste.


A NPDES permitted POTW is a POTW that discharges treated wastewater and is permitted to do so. This contrasts with a non-NPDES permitted POTW, which may accept the same types of wastes as a permitted POTW but does not discharge the treated wastewater (such as, non-discharging lagoons that use evaporative techniques and/or land application).


This mapping application only includes NPDES permitted POTWs.


Public Water System (PWS)

A public water system provides water for human consumption through pipes or other constructed conveyances to at least 15 service connections or serves an average of at least 25 people for at least 60 days a year. A public water system may be publicly or privately owned. The three types of public water systems include: Community Water System (CWS), Non-Transient Non-Community Water System (NTNCWS), and Transient Non-Community Water System (TNCWS). This mapping application only includes Community Water Systems.


Service Area/Service Area Boundary

The area encompassing all service connections of a given Public Water System or Publicly Owned Treatment Works. See Drinking Water Service Areas and Wastewater Service Areas for detailed information.  

 

Utility

A term used interchangeably with “Public Water System”, “Community Water System”, and “NPDES POTW” to encompass both drinking water systems and wastewater facilities.

Caveats and Limitations


Appropriate Uses of Water ICAT

Water ICAT provides technical assistance providers and related entities a data-driven resource to screen for utilities that may have water infrastructure needs and may benefit from related assistance. Although the term “need” is used through Water ICAT, this tool is not meant to label systems. Instead, “need” provides a conceptual framework for using and interacting with data within Water ICAT.


Water ICAT is just one of several resources that can be used for this purpose and is intended to complement rather than replace existing resources.


Additionally, Water ICAT incorporates enforcement and compliance data, however, Water ICAT is not intended to be used as an enforcement targeting tool.

 

Water Infrastructure Not Included in Water ICAT

Water ICAT does not include all types of water infrastructure critical to a community. At present, Water ICAT only screens for potential assistance needs at Community Water Systems (drinking water systems) and National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permitted Publicly Owned Treatment Works (public wastewater facilities). This is primarily due to limited or nonexistent nationally comprehensive data for other types of water infrastructure, such as, stormwater systems* and septic systems. However, as new data become available, additional water infrastructure may be incorporated into Water ICAT.

 

*EPA is undergoing efforts to improve the accuracy of the wastewater data. As such, Water ICAT may include a few municipal separate storm sewer systems (MS4s) but does not contain a comprehensive dataset, so the tool should not be used to screen for potential water infrastructure needs at MS4 facilities.

 

Screening-level Indicators

Water ICAT provides screening-level proxies for assistance needs. The caveats and limitations associated with these proxies are described more below.


Enforcement and Compliance Data

While enforcement and compliance (violation) data can be valuable indictors of underlying challenges at a utility, violation data are lagging indicators. This means that data are backwards looking, and facilities may have already resolved any potential underling infrastructure or capacity challenges that were causing violations and/or enforcement actions.

 

In addition to violation data being inherently backwards looking, violations can stem from a variety of root causes unique to a given utility that may not be related to infrastructure or capacity challenges.

 

Infrastructure Funding Data

At present, only Clean Water State Revolving Fund (CWSRF) and Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) data are included in Water ICAT. However, there are several other potential sources of funding a community may pursue to fund water infrastructure projects such as private funding or financing sources, utility revenues, and state or federal government agency sources. Funding information from these sources are not included within Water ICAT due to data availability.

 

Demographic and Economic Data

Caveats and limitations associated with the demographic and economic data primarily stem from the availability of precise and accurate service area spatial data. See, “Service Area Boundaries and Demographic/Economic Data” subsection, below.

 

Additional Factors/Considerations When Screening for Utilities with Potential Assistance Needs﻿

In addition to the discussion above, there are other factors that may impact a utility’s assistance need(s) including:

  1. A utility may already be receiving assistance.
  2. A utility may not wish to receive assistance or have the capacity to accept support.
  3. The screening level proxies used were not a good fit for the on the ground conditions/situations at a particular facility.

 

As with any screening tool, Water ICAT cannot address all the considerations that may be relevant to a given situation because of the factors listed above. Therefore, it is not appropriate to solely rely on this screening tool for key decisions. It is recommended to consult with other sources of information, including working with entities that have local knowledge.

 

Service Area Boundaries and Demographic/Economic Data

Service area boundaries, representing the geographic area that a drinking water or wastewater utility serve, are valuable when wanting to understand the make-up of the community served by a system, such as whether the system serves rural or low-income populations, among other available demographic and economic characteristics populated within Water ICAT.

 

Despite the enormous value of service area boundaries in this context, service area spatial data for drinking water systems and wastewater facilities are in different stages of development/availability, impacting the precision and accuracy of the demographic/economic characteristic data provided for each utility in this tool.

 

  1. Drinking water systems: Most drinking water systems included within Water ICAT have spatial boundary data that enable demographic and economic characteristics to be derived at the service area boundary scale. A small percentage of systems included within Water ICAT do not have spatial boundary data; these systems are displayed as points on the map. For these, demographic and economic characteristic data are not available within Water ICAT due to insufficient information to discern the bounds of the service area and the corresponding population characteristics served by the system. Visit the Drinking Water Service Area Boundary page to learn more about drinking water service area boundaries.


  1. Wastewater facilities: The point location (latitude/longitude) of the wastewater treatment plant is used as the spatial component for discerning demographic and economic characteristics within a buffer zone around the treatment plant. Water ICAT calculates demographic and economic characteristics within three buffer zones around the treatment plant: 1-mile, 3-mile, and 5-mile. Buffer zones are used for wastewater facilities because there are currently no nationally comprehensive datasets for the areas served by wastewater facilities. Although buffer zones are not a replacement for having spatial boundary data, it does provide a starting point understanding characteristics of the population within a certain proximity of the treatment plant. Note that only 3-mi buffer values are shown in the map. 1-mi and 5-mi buffer values are available in the map pop-up and data table. Visit the Wastewater Spatial Data page to learn more about wastewater facility spatial data.

How to Use Water ICAT


The steps below describe the process for using Water ICAT.


General Notes
  1. Unless otherwise specified, filters apply cumulatively. This means that only utilities meeting ALL selected filter criteria will be shown.
  2. Based on the user's desired "sample size" (e.g., how many utilities the user wants to work with for further evaluation/analysis), it's recommended to monitor the system/facility counter on the map page, showing how many utilities meet the selected filter criteria. As more filters are applied, the number of utilities will reduce. This can be a helpful indicator of when to add/remove filters.


Step 1 – Apply desired filters
  1. Filters are grouped into 4 categories: General System Characteristics, Demographic Characteristics, Compliance Characteristics, and Water Infrastructure Funding History.
  2. A user should select any filters that are relevant to their screening goals.


Step 2 – Turn on other map layers for additional context
  1. Viewing additional map layers available within the tool or adding in your own map layers does not further filter the data.
  2. Turning on select map layers can provide additional context for further analysis/evaluation.


Step 3 – Print map and/or export results
  1. Printing the resulting map and/or exporting the screening results can be useful if/when conducting further analysis or evaluation of utilities.


Step 4 – Conduct further analysis/evaluation
  1. Because the results from Water ICAT are "screening level", it's strongly recommended that the user conduct further analysis/evaluation of the utilities identified using Water ICAT.
  2. For example, the user may choose to discuss results with entities familiar with the utilities before beginning potential next steps of outreach to those utilities OR the user may select to perform additional analysis on the exported data.

config.text:
Tool Design


This section describes how Water ICAT enables users to screen for potential need.

 

Does Water ICAT create a single index value for need?

No, Water ICAT does not create a single index value of need for each utility. Instead, the Water ICAT includes data filters organized by data type (such as, compliance related data, demographic and economic characteristic data, infrastructure funding data, etc.) that a user can select from based on their screening goals.


What data categories are included within Water ICAT?

Water ICAT includes four primary types of data: (1) “General Utility Characteristics”, (2) “Demographic/Economic Characteristics”, (3) “Enforcement/Compliance Characteristics”, and (4) “Water Infrastructure Funding History”.

 

  1. General Utility Characteristics includes baseline utility characteristics such as location, population size served or utility size, infrastructure type (for wastewater).


  1. Demographic/Economic Characteristics includes Census and American Community Survey data such as rural, income, and unemployment, among others. These data are included for utilities when adequate spatial data are available to know the actual or approximated service area for a utility. These data provide insight into the population that comprises a utility’s (actual or approximated) service area.


  1. Enforcement/Compliance Characteristics includes compliance data for the most recent official reporting period AND historical compliance data. Root cause(s) of a given violation will be unique to each utility and could be due to capacity related factors, such as staffing challenges, difficulty keeping up with regulatory changes, infrastructure related factors (including inadequate maintenance), or aging infrastructure. While it's not possible to discern a specific root cause with enforcement/compliance data alone, these data can provide users a starting point for identifying utilities that are having challenges significant enough to result in noncompliance.


  1. Water Infrastructure Funding History are included to enable users to know if a utility has received SRF water infrastructure funding in the past. Past receipt of water infrastructure funding can provide insight into a utility’s capacity to successfully identify, apply for, and receive funding. Additionally, some assistance providers may wish to prioritize utilities that have not received funding from a particular source in the past. While it can be helpful to have this information, there are other sources of water infrastructure funding that utilities may use beyond what is incorporated within Water ICAT.

 

Each of these data types have their own caveats and limitations; visit Caveats and Limitations for more information.

What is the Water Infrastructure and Capacity Assessment Tool (ICAT)?

Water ICAT is a mapping application that supports the identification of drinking water and wastewater utilities that may benefit from water infrastructure technical assistance or capacity development assistance to provide affordable, safe water to communities.


Water ICAT incorporates utility-level compliance, demographic, and water infrastructure funding data, allowing users to make map filter selections best suited to their screening goals.


Need More Information?

To learn more about Water ICAT, including information on design and use, service areas, and data sources, visit the Tool Information Page.

Drinking Water System Spatial Data


Water ICAT incorporates spatial data in two ways for drinking water systems. Water ICAT uses actual and modeled service area boundary data (when available) and uses point locations for systems that do not have boundary data.


What is the difference between “spatial boundary” and “point location” data in this context?

When referring to spatial boundaries, this is referring to a physical boundary of a water system. When viewing the Water ICAT map, systems with spatial boundary data will appear as polygons. The polygon outline indicates the approximate physical boundary of a drinking water system. Water system boundaries are irregular and DO NOT follow the boundaries of a political/geographic unit. For example, multiple water systems often serve a single county; these systems will not overlap but will each provide water service to a portion of the county. Water system boundaries can be thought of as puzzle pieces.

 

By contrast, point locations are used when boundaries of a drinking water system are not known. Point locations can be used in these cases because all public water systems must report information about at least one area they serve (e.g., a county, city, zip code, tribe that is within the system’s service area). While this is helpful information to know generally where a system is located, it does not tell us the physical boundaries of a system.


Spatial Boundary Data (SAB)

EPA has developed a community water system service area boundary (SAB) dataset for active CWS. This dataset is comprised of system boundaries that have been obtained directly from states, and when not available, modeled boundaries for the remaining CWS.

 

As shown in the figure and as described above, systems with spatial boundary data are shown as polygons, representing the physical boundaries (service area) of the system.


Technical details on EPA’s methodology for developing the drinking water service area boundary dataset can be found here: Community Water System Service Areas.


Point Data

Some drinking water systems are not included in EPA CWS service area boundary dataset. In these cases, Water ICAT uses area served data a from the Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS). Area served data may be reported at the county, city, zip code, tribe, or territory scales.


To include these water systems on the map, Water ICAT places a point at the centroid of the reported area(s) served.

 

Spatial and Demographic/Economic Data

Water ICAT allows users to filter for drinking water systems based on demographic and economic characteristics within the service area. This requires the availability of spatial data (e.g., where a water system is) as demographic and economic characteristics are derived from population characteristics within a certain area.

 

With this, only systems that have service area boundary data will have demographic and economic characteristics derived.

___

Image: Screenshot of Water ICAT showing community water systems that have spatial boundary data (blue outlines) versus CWS that are shown as points (points representing the centroid of the area(s) that system serves).

﻿Wastewater (POTW) Spatial Data


In the absence of service area boundaries, Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTWs) are displayed as points referring to the locations of the wastewater treatment plants.


The POTW collection systems are not mapped due to data availability. In the absence of boundary data, Water ICAT uses latitude/longitude contained within ICIS-NPDES (Integrated Compliance Information System-National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System) for each POTW included in Water ICAT.  


Demographic and Economic Data

In the absence of boundary data, Water ICAT provides information on demographic and economic characteristics within a certain proximity of the treatment plant. Water ICAT provides demographic and economic characteristics within a 1-3-5 mi proximity (or buffer) around the treatment plant. Note that only 3-mi buffer values are shown in the map. 1-mi and 5-mi buffer values are available in the map pop-up and data table.


These data should not be interpreted as representative of a POTW service area.

The primary data incorporated into Water ICAT to support screening are general system characteristics, demographic and economic characteristics, enforcement and compliance characteristics, and water infrastructure funding/financing data.

Map Functionalities


This tool is interactive and contains widgets that allow the user to perform various functions.


Select

Use this widget to select and to filter for water utilities within a drawn geographic boundary. This widget can help users wanting to limit screening results to those within a specified area. This widget can be used before applying map filters or after applying map filters, depending on screening goals. 


Filter the map

Use this widget to filter for utilities that meet desired screening criteria.


Turn on/off map layers

Use this widget to turn on or turn off map layers.


View map legend

Use this widget to view and understand map "symbology", or what the colors/symbols used in the map represent. The legend only populates for map layers currently turned on.


Add your own data/map layers

This widget allows the user to add custom data/map layers to their CURRENT session; data/maps added to a session DO NOT save for future sessions.


Change map basemap

This widget allows the user to change the map basemap. Options include streets, aerial imagery, and topographic basemaps, among others.


Print/export map image

﻿This widget allows the user to print an image of the map, including the map legend, title, and other configurable layout options.

About


Water ICAT is a mapping application that supports the identification of water utilities that may benefit from water infrastructure technical assistance or capacity development assistance to provide affordable, safe water to communities.

About


Water ICAT is a mapping application that supports the identification of water utilities that may benefit from water infrastructure technical assistance or capacity development assistance to provide affordable, safe water to communities and to achieve resilient water utilities.


Water ICAT provides a nationally consistent, data driven approach to users such as technical assistance providers and programs, helping them screen for utilities for outreach and ultimately support.

 

It does this by providing a tool that is,


  1. Integrated: Aggregates compliance, environmental justice, and funding data at the utility scale, helping users consider a variety of factors that may influence need.
  2. Accessible: Integrates data from sources that often require greater expertise to view, integrate, and use, displaying those data in a way that is easier for non-technical audiences to use and understand.
  3. Fit for Purpose: Selects the most pertinent data and associated map filter options for screening for water utilities with potential assistance needs.

Key Terms


Key terms used throughout this application include:


Community Water System (CWS): A type of public water system that supplies water to the same population year-round.

 

Facility: A term used interchangeably with “Publicly Owned Treatment Works” or “wastewater facility.”

 

National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Permitted Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTW):


  • A POTW is a treatment plant owned by a State or municipality and is designed to provide treatment (including recycling and reclamation) of municipal sewage and industrial waste.
  • A NPDES permitted POTW is a POTW that discharges treated wastewater and is permitted to do so. This contrasts with a non-NPDES permitted POTW, which may accept the same types of wastes as a permitted POTW but does not discharge the treated wastewater (such as, non-discharging lagoons that use evaporative techniques and/or land application).
  • This mapping application only includes NPDES permitted POTWs.


Public Water System (PWS): A public water system provides water for human consumption through pipes or other constructed conveyances to at least 15 service connections or serves an average of at least 25 people for at least 60 days a year. A public water system may be publicly or privately owned. The three types of public water systems include: Community Water System (CWS), Non-Transient Non-Community Water System (NTNCWS), and Transient Non-Community Water System (TNCWS).

 

  • This mapping application only includes Community Water Systems.


Service Area/Service Area Boundary: The area encompassing all service connections of a given Public Water System or Publicly Owned Treatment Works. See Drinking Water Service Areas and Wastewater Service Areas for detailed information.  

 

Utility: A term used interchangeably with “Public Water System”, “Community Water System”, and “NPDES POTW” to encompass both drinking water systems and wastewater facilities.

Water Infrastructure Types Included


Water ICAT includes water infrastructure types where there are high quality, nationally comprehensive data.

 

Currently, these types include:


  • Drinking Water: Community Water Systems (CWS) and
  • Wastewater: National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permitted Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTWs).


Are there plans to add additional water infrastructure information/types in the future? The limiting factor in not including other infrastructure types (such as, stormwater systems**, private domestic wells, septic systems, and non-discharging wastewater facilities) is national data availability. As data availability improves, more water infrastructure types may be added to this tool.

 

**NOTE: EPA is undergoing efforts to improve the accuracy of the wastewater data. As such, Water ICAT may include a few municipal separate storm sewer systems (MS4s) but does not contain a comprehensive dataset, so the tool should not be used to screen for potential water infrastructure needs at MS4 facilities.

Tool Design


This section describes how Water ICAT enables users to screen for potential need.

 

Does Water ICAT create a single index value for need?

No, Water ICAT does not create a single index value of need for each utility. Instead, the Water ICAT includes data filters organized by data type (such as, compliance related data, community characteristic data, infrastructure funding data, etc.) that a user can select from based on their screening goals.


What categories of data are included within Water ICAT?

Water ICAT includes four primary types of data: (1) “General Utility Characteristics”, (2) “Community Characteristics”, (3) “Enforcement/Compliance Characteristics”, and (4) “Water Infrastructure Funding History”.

 

  1. General Utility Characteristics includes baseline utility characteristics such as location, population size served or utility size, infrastructure type (for wastewater).
  2. Community Characteristics includes environmental justice, disadvantaged community, and other socioeconomic/demographic characteristic data. These data are included for utilities when adequate spatial data are available to know the actual or approximated service area for a utility. These data provide insight into the population that comprises a utility’s (actual or approximated) service area. Utilities serving populations that are majority disadvantaged or with potential environmental justice concerns may face unique and compounding challenges. Such utilities may have capacity and resource limitations or may have experienced historical underinvestment.
  3. Enforcement/Compliance Characteristics includes compliance data for the most recent official reporting period AND historical compliance data. Root cause(s) of a given violation will be unique to each utility and could be due to capacity related factors, such as staffing challenges, difficulty keeping up with regulatory changes, infrastructure related factors (including inadequate maintenance), or aging infrastructure. While it's not possible to discern a specific root cause with enforcement/compliance data alone, these data can provide users a starting point for identifying utilities that are having challenges significant enough to result in noncompliance.
  4. Water Infrastructure Funding History are included to enable users to know if a utility has received SRF water infrastructure funding in the past. Past receipt of water infrastructure funding can provide insight into a utility’s capacity to successfully identify, apply for, and receive funding. Additionally, some assistance providers may wish to prioritize utilities that have not received funding from a particular source in the past. While it can be helpful to have this information, there are other sources of water infrastructure funding that utilities may use beyond what is incorporated within Water ICAT.

 

Each of these data types have their own caveats and limitations; visit Caveats and Limitations for more information.

The primary data incorporated into Water ICAT to support screening are general system characteristics, community characteristics, enforcement and compliance characteristics, and water infrastructure funding/financing data.

Caveats and Limitations


Appropriate Uses of Water ICAT

Water ICAT provides technical assistance providers and related entities a data-driven resource to screen for utilities that may have water infrastructure needs and may benefit from related assistance. Although the term “need” is used through Water ICAT, this tool is not meant to label systems. Instead, “need” provides a conceptual framework for using and interacting with data within Water ICAT.

 

Water ICAT is just one of several resources that can be used for this purpose and is intended to complement rather than replace existing resources.

 

Additionally, Water ICAT incorporates enforcement and compliance data, however, Water ICAT is not intended to be used as an enforcement targeting tool.

 

Water Infrastructure Not Included in Water ICAT

Water ICAT does not include all types of water infrastructure critical to a community. At present, Water ICAT only screens for potential assistance needs at Community Water Systems (drinking water systems) and National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permitted Publicly Owned Treatment Works (public wastewater facilities). This is primarily due to limited or nonexistent nationally comprehensive data for other types of water infrastructure, such as, stormwater systems** and septic systems. However, as new data become available, additional water infrastructure may be incorporated into Water ICAT.

 

**NOTE: EPA is undergoing efforts to improve the accuracy of the wastewater data. As such, Water ICAT may include a few municipal separate storm sewer systems (MS4s) but does not contain a comprehensive dataset, so the tool should not be used to screen for potential water infrastructure needs at MS4 facilities.

 

Screening-level Indicators

Water ICAT provides screening-level proxies for assistance needs. The caveats and limitations associated with these proxies are described more below.


Enforcement and Compliance Data

While enforcement and compliance (violation) data can be valuable indictors of underlying challenges at a utility, violation data are lagging indicators. This means that data are backwards looking, and facilities may have already resolved any potential underling infrastructure or capacity challenges that were causing violations and/or enforcement actions.

 

In addition to violation data being inherently backwards looking, violations can stem from a variety of root causes unique to a given utility that may not be related to infrastructure or capacity challenges.

 

Infrastructure Funding Data

At present, only Clean Water State Revolving Fund (CWSRF) and Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) data are included in Water ICAT. However, there are several other potential sources of funding a community may pursue to fund water infrastructure projects such as private funding or financing sources, utility revenues, and state or federal government agency sources. Funding information from these sources are not included within Water ICAT due to data availability.

 

Environmental Justice/Disadvantaged Community Data

Caveats and limitations associated with the environmental justice and disadvantaged community data primarily stem from the availability of precise and accurate service area spatial data. See, “Service Area Boundaries and Environmental Justice Data” subsection, below.


Additionally, Water ICAT does not include or integrate state specific disadvantaged community (DAC) criteria or definitions. Instead, Water ICAT includes a variety of commonly used measures of disadvantaged such as the Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST) DAC definition, the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) DAC criteria, among others.

 

Additional Factors/Considerations When Screening for Utilities with Potential Assistance Needs﻿

In addition to the discussion above, there are other factors that may impact a utility’s assistance need(s) including:

  1. A utility may already be receiving assistance.
  2. A utility may not wish to receive assistance or have the capacity to accept support.
  3. The screening level proxies used were not a good fit for the on the ground conditions/situations at a particular facility.

 

As with any screening tool, Water ICAT cannot address all the considerations that may be relevant to a given situation because of the factors listed above. Therefore, it is not appropriate to solely rely on this screening tool for key decisions. It is recommended to consult with other sources of information, including working with entities that have local knowledge.

 

Service Area Boundaries and Environmental Justice Data

Service area boundaries, representing the geographic area that a drinking water or wastewater utility serve, are valuable when wanting to understand community characteristics (such as, environmental justice or disadvantaged community characteristics) within a service area.

 

Despite the enormous value of service area boundaries in this context, service area spatial data for drinking water systems and wastewater facilities are in different stages of development/availability, impacting the precision and accuracy of the community characteristic data provided for each utility in this tool.

 

  1. Drinking water systems: Most drinking water systems included within Water ICAT have spatial boundary data that enable community characteristics to be derived at the service area boundary scale. A small percentage of systems included within Water ICAT do not have spatial boundary data; these systems are displayed as points on the map. For these, community characteristic data are not available within Water ICAT due to insufficient information to discern the bounds of the service area and the corresponding population characteristics served by the system.


Visit the Drinking Water Service Area Boundary page to learn more about drinking water service area boundaries.


  1. Wastewater facilities: The point location (latitude/longitude) of the wastewater treatment plant is used as the spatial component for discerning community characteristics within a buffer zone around the treatment plant. Water ICAT calculates community characteristics within three buffer zones around the treatment plant: 1-mile, 3-mile, and 5-mile. Buffer zones are used for wastewater facilities because there are currently no nationally comprehensive datasets for the areas served by wastewater facilities. Although buffer zones are not a replacement for having spatial boundary data, it does provide a starting point understanding characteristics of the population within a certain proximity of the treatment plant. Note that only 3-mi buffer values are shown in the map. 1-mi and 5-mi buffer values are available in the map pop-up and data table.


Visit the Wastewater Spatial Data page to learn more about wastewater facility spatial data.

﻿Appropriate Use as a Screening Tool


While data are powerful aids in identifying where potential water infrastructure needs may exist across states, tribes, and territories – this tool should be used for screening purposes for potential technical assistance versus a definitive indication of need.


As discussed on the Tool Design and Caveats and Limitations pages, Water ICAT uses indicators of need as opposed to direct measures. Because of these limitations, Water ICAT should only be used for screening.

 

What is an example of appropriate use as a screening tool? Outreach for technical assistance could be a common use of Water ICAT. In this use scenario:


  1. Users select their screening requirements using the available map filters to identify utilities with potential assistance needs. The result is a list of utilities with potential needs.
  2. Users then "ground-truth" and gain additional context about the utilities identified (such as, more detailed information about their specific needs, challenges, and communities served). One way this can be done is by speaking with the EPA Region OR the state/tribe/territory where the utility is located. This can result in helpful context, for example, a utility may already be receiving help from another entity OR the facility may have just received funding to address its infrastructure need. The result of this “ground-truthing” is a further refined list of communities that may require assistance.
  3. After getting additional context on the screening list, users can reach out to the refined list of utilities to begin the discussion on helping the community access beneficial resources.

 

What is an example of inappropriate use? An example of inappropriate use would be any application that characterizes the screening list of utilities as having definitive needs, WITHOUT having first consulted additional information and/or local knowledge.

 

Note: To learn about EPA assistance resources, visit the "Assistance Resources" page.

Drinking Water System Spatial Data


Water ICAT incorporates spatial data in two ways for drinking water systems. Water ICAT uses actual and modeled service area boundary data (when available) and uses point locations for systems that do not have boundary data.


What is the difference between “spatial boundary” and “point location” data in this context?

When referring to spatial boundaries, this is referring to a physical boundary of a water system. When viewing Water ICAT map, systems with spatial boundary data will appear as polygons. The polygon outline indicates the physical boundary of a drinking water system.

 

By contrast, point locations are used when boundaries of a drinking water system are not known. Point locations can be used in these cases because all public water systems must report information about at least one area they serve (e.g., a county, city, zip code, tribe that is within the system’s service area). While this is helpful information to know generally where a system is located, it does not tell us the physical boundaries of a system. Water system boundaries are irregular and DO NOT follow the boundaries of a political/geographic unit. For example, multiple water systems often serve a single county; these systems will not overlap but will each provide water service to a portion of the county. Water system boundaries can be thought of as puzzle pieces.


Spatial Boundary Data (SAB)

EPA has developed a community water system service area boundary (SAB) dataset for active CWS. This dataset is comprised of system boundaries that have been obtained directly from states, and when not available, modeled boundaries for the remaining CWS.

 

As shown in the figure and as described above, systems with spatial boundary data are shown as polygons, representing the physical boundaries (service area) of the system.


Technical details on EPA’s methodology for developing the drinking water service area boundary dataset can be found here: Community Water System Service Areas.


Point Data

Some drinking water systems do not have available service area boundary data. In these cases, Water ICAT uses data from SDWIS (Safe Drinking Water Information System) on area(s) that are within a system’s service area. Area served data may be reported at the county, city, zip code, tribe, or territory scales.

 

To be able to include these water systems on the map, Water ICAT places a point at the centroid of the reported area(s) served.

 

Spatial and Environmental Justice/Disadvantaged Community Data

Water ICAT allows users to filter for drinking water systems that service areas that are identified as disadvantaged (DAC) or with potential environmental justice (EJ) concerns. This requires the availability of spatial data (e.g., where a water system is) as EJ and DAC characteristics are derived from population characteristics within a certain area.

 

With this, only systems that have spatial boundary data will have EJ/DAC characteristics derived.

﻿Wastewater (POTW) Spatial Data


In the absence of service area boundaries, Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTWs) are displayed as points referring to the locations of the wastewater treatment plants.


The POTW collection systems are not mapped due to data availability. In the absence of boundary data, Water ICAT uses latitude/longitude contained within ICIS-NPDES (Integrated Compliance Information System-National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System) for each POTW included in Water ICAT.   


Environmental Justice/Disadvantaged Community Data

In the absence of boundary data to discern EJ/DAC characteristics within a service area, Water ICAT provides information on community characteristics within a certain proximity of the treatment plant. Water ICAT provides EJ/DAC characteristics within a 1-3-5 mi proximity (or buffer) around the treatment plant. Providing EJ/DAC characteristics within buffer zones around the POTW provides users a helpful starting point for further evaluation of POTW potential DAC/EJ concerns. Note that only 3-mi buffer values are shown in the map. 1-mi and 5-mi buffer values are available in the map pop-up and data table.


These data should not be interpreted as representative of a POTW service area.

Map Functionalities


This tool is interactive and contains widgets that allow the user to perform various functions.


  • Select: Use this widget to select and to filter for water utilities within a drawn geographic boundary. This widget can help users wanting to limit screening results to those within a specified area. This widget can be used before applying map filters or after applying map filters, depending on screening goals.  


  • Filter the map: Use this widget to filter for utilities that meet desired screening criteria.


  • Turn on/off map layers: Use this widget to turn on or turn off map layers.


  • View map legend: Use this widget to view and understand map "symbology", or what the colors/symbols used in the map represent. The legend only populates for map layers currently turned on.


  • Add your own data/map layers: This widget allows the user to add custom data/map layers to their CURRENT session; data/maps added to a session DO NOT save for future sessions.


  • Change map basemap: This widget allows the user to change the map basemap. Options include streets, aerial imagery, and topographic basemaps, among others.


  • Print/export map image: This widget allows the user to print an image of the map, including the map legend, title, and other configurable layout options.

How to Use Water ICAT (Steps)


The steps below describe the process for using Water ICAT.


General Notes:

  1. Unless otherwise specified, filters apply cumulatively. This means that only utilities meeting ALL selected filter criteria will be shown.
  2. Based on the user's desired "sample size" (e.g., how many utilities the user wants to work with for further evaluation/analysis), it's recommended to monitor the system/facility counter on the map page, showing how many utilities meet the selected filter criteria. As more filters are applied, the number of utilities will reduce. This can be a helpful indicator of when to add/remove filters.


Step 1 – Apply desired filters

  1. Filters are grouped into 4 categories: General System Characteristics, Community Characteristics, Compliance Characteristics, and Water Infrastructure Funding History.
  2. A user should select any filters that are relevant to their screening goals.


Step 2 – Turn on other map layers for additional context

  1. Viewing additional map layers available within the tool (e.g., environmental justice, climate change, or tribal lands layers) or adding in your own map layers does not further filter the data.
  2. Turning on select map layers can provide additional context for further analysis/evaluation.


Step 3 – Print map and/or export results

  1. Printing the resulting map and/or exporting the screening results can be useful if/when conducting further analysis or evaluation of utilities.


Step 4 – Conduct further analysis/evaluation

  1. Because the results from Water ICAT are "screening level", it's strongly recommended that the user conduct further analysis/evaluation of the utilities identified using Water ICAT.
  2. For example, the user may choose to discuss results with entities familiar with the utilities before beginning potential next steps of outreach to those utilities OR the user may select to perform additional analysis on the exported data.

How to Reset Filters


To reset map filters, use the "reset button" located on the bottom right corner of each filter category.


Each filter category (e.g., “General”, “Community”, “Compliance”, etc.) has its own reset button as shown on the figure. If filters are applied under more than one category, this step must be done for EACH category.

What Systems/Facilities Populate in the Data Table?


﻿The "View and Export Data" page allows users to view and export all utilities meeting selected filters.


The map and data tables are dynamically linked. This means that the data table reflects all map filters a user has currently applied.


Conversely, if additional filters selections are made using table filter functionalities, the map will reflect these changes.


Important note for drinking water tables: Because there are two tables for drinking water systems - a table for systems with spatial data and a table for systems without spatial data - users must repeat filter selections made within the table view, across both tables. If this step is not taken, when viewing the map, only one layer will show the additional filter selections made (the layer for which additional filters were selected within the table view).


﻿Example: The wastewater map was filtered for all systems in Region 1. This populates 436 wastewater facilities. When navigating to the Data Tables and Export page, only those filtered facilities display in the table. This is indicated by the "Total: 436" seen on the data table page. This value matches the total count of facilities shown on the map page.

Lead and Copper Rule Violations (5-years, Count of Quarters)

Definition: Indicates the number of quarters in the last 5-years (20 quarters) a system had at least one Lead and Copper Rule violation (whether or not the violation has returned to compliance).


Lead and copper enter drinking water primarily through plumbing materials. Exposure to lead and copper may cause health problems ranging from stomach distress to brain damage.


In 1991, EPA published a regulation to control lead and copper in drinking water. This regulation is known as the Lead and Copper Rule (also referred to as the LCR). Since 1991 the LCR has undergone various revisions.


The treatment technique for the rule requires systems to monitor drinking water at customer taps. If lead concentrations exceed an action level of 15 ppb or copper concentrations exceed an action level of 1.3 ppm in more than 10% of customer taps sampled, the system must undertake a number of additional actions to control corrosion.


If the action level for lead is exceeded, the system must also inform the public about steps they should take to protect their health and may have to replace lead service lines under their control.


Learn more about the Lead and Copper Rule, here: https://www.epa.gov/dwreginfo/lead-and-copper-rule.

Effluent Parameter Violations (Categories)

Definition: Indicates the corresponding pollutant category for effluent parameters violated at least once during most recent official reporting period, "Current Reporting Period (Federal Fiscal Year-Quarter)".


Pollutant categories include:


Metals - All metals parameters. Hexavalent or trivalent metals and metals in ionic form (e.g., hexavalent chromium and aluminum, ion) are included, but metal compounds (e.g., calcium chloride) are not included.

Nitrogen - All parameters for total nitrogen, organic nitrogen, total Kjeldahl nitrogen, nitrite, nitrate, and ammonia.

Organic Enrichment - Parameters for biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD).

Pathogen Indicators - Parameters for total coliform, streptococci, and enteric.

Phosphorus - Phosphorus and phosphate parameters. 

Clean Water Act Priority Pollutants - The 126 pollutants that EPA currently defines as priority pollutants. 

CERCLA Hazardous Substances - Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) hazardous substances are substances that are considered severely harmful to human health and the environment. Many are commonly used substances which are harmless in their normal uses, but are quite dangerous when released. They are defined in terms of those substances either specifically designated as hazardous under the Superfund law, or those substances identified under other laws. Superfund's definition of a hazardous substance includes the following: Any element, compound, mixture, solution, or substance designated as hazardous under section 102 of CERCLA.

  1. Any hazardous substance designated under section 311(b)(2)(a) of the Clean Water Act (CWA), or any toxic pollutant listed under section 307(a) of the CWA. There are over 400 substances designated as either hazardous or toxic under the CWA.
  2. Any hazardous waste having the characteristics identified or listed under section 3001 of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. Any hazardous air pollutant listed under section 112 of the Clean Air Act, as amended. There are over 200 substances listed as hazardous air pollutants under the Clean Air Act (CAA).
  3. Any imminently hazardous chemical substance or mixture which the EPA Administrator has "taken action under" section 7 of the Toxic Substances Control Act.

TRI Chemicals - All pollutants that are associated with chemicals that are reported to EPA's Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) Program.

Solids - Parameters for suspended and settable solids. This category does not include chemical-specific solids, such as suspended copper.

Wastewater Flow - All wastewater flow parameters for measuring wastewater flows in millions of gallons per day, gallons per day, and gallons per minute.

Temperature - Parameters for measuring wastewater temperature in degrees Fahrenheit and Celsius.

Radionuclides - All parameters measuring specific radionuclides such as Uranium and Radium isotopes, as well as radioactivity not specific to a particular isotope, including gross alpha and gross beta radiation. 

Color - All parameters measuring color in wastewater. Color measurements may be reported using a variety of units, such as Platinum Cobalt (Pt-Co) units or pound/ton produced.

Whole Effluent Toxicity - Parameters measuring Whole Effluent Toxicity (WET) in wastewater. WET refers to the aggregate toxic effect to aquatic organisms from all pollutants contained in a facility’s wastewater. 

Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) - PFAS are a group of man-made chemicals that includes Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), Perfluorooctane Sulfonate (PFOS), GenX, and many other chemicals. PFAS have been manufactured and used in a variety of industries around the globe, including in the United States since the 1940s. The chemicals are very persistent in the environment and in the human body – meaning they don’t break down and they can accumulate over time. There is evidence that exposure to PFAS can lead to adverse human health effects.


More information on pollutant categories can be found, here, under "Pollutant Category (Wastewater Only)".

Connecting Communities with Resources


Some users of Water ICAT may be able to provide assistance themselves (e.g., may be a technical assistance provider). Other users may not be an assistance provider, but instead an entity that works to connect communities with assistance providers. For the latter, EPA has a water infrastructure technical assistance program called WaterTA. Through EPA's WaterTA program, communities can receive assistance on activities ranging lead service line inventories, capacity development support, compliance assistance, funding applications, and more. Below are helpful links to learn more about EPA's WaterTA program:


  • About EPA's WaterTA program: https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure/water-technical-assistance-waterta
  • List of WaterTA programs: https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure/water-technical-assistance-programs
  • WaterTA Request Form (submit a request for TA): https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure/forms/water-technical-assistance-request-form


Additionally, states often have their own water infrastructure technical assistance programs as well as other federal agencies such as USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture), HUD (Housing and Urban Development), and IHS (Indian Health Service).


Finally, the USEPA maintains Water Finance Clearinghouse, a web‐based portal that can help communities locate information and resources to inform on decisions about drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater infrastructure needs: https://www.epa.gov/waterfinancecenter/water-finance-clearinghouse-portal.

config.text: Community Water System Display Note

This map uses a combination of polygons and points to show the locations of drinking water systems.


Polygons are used when service area boundary data are available for a given system, and indicate the approximate area served by a system.


Points are used when boundary data are not available. Points indicate the centroid of the county, tribe, or territory a system serves. When zoomed out, point locations display as clusters, indicating the number of systems within that cluster. Zooming in will reveal the individual points/systems. In instances when more than one system share a service area centroid, the points will remain clustered.


For more information on mapping of drinking water systems, visit the Spatial Data information page.
Community Water System Data Tables Note

There are two community water system tables available for viewing/filtering/exporting.


The Systems with Boundaries table is associated with the polygon map layer (e.g., systems with available service area boundary data).


The Systems without Boundaries table is associated with the point map layer (e.g., systems without available service area boundary data).


Notes:

  1. Available fields/attributes are identical across both tables.
  2. Filters applied to one community water system table do not automatically apply to the second community water system table. Filter selections must be manually repeated across both tables.

About


Water ICAT is a mapping application that supports the identification of water utilities that may benefit from water infrastructure technical assistance or capacity development assistance to provide affordable, safe water to communities.


Water ICAT provides a nationally consistent, data driven approach to users such as technical assistance providers and programs, helping them screen for utilities for outreach and ultimately support.

 

It does this by providing a tool that is,


  1. Integrated: Aggregates compliance, demographic, and funding data at the utility scale, helping users consider a variety of factors that may influence need.
  2. Accessible: Integrates data from sources that often require greater expertise to view, integrate, and use, displaying those data in a way that is easier for non-technical audiences to use and understand.
  3. Fit for Purpose: Selects the most pertinent data and associated map filter options for screening for water utilities with potential assistance needs.

Key Terms


Community Water System (CWS)

A type of public water system that supplies water to the same population year-round.

 

Facility

A term used interchangeably with “Publicly Owned Treatment Works” or “wastewater facility.”

 

National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Permitted Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTW)

A POTW is a treatment plant owned by a State or municipality and is designed to provide treatment (including recycling and reclamation) of municipal sewage and industrial waste.


A NPDES permitted POTW is a POTW that discharges treated wastewater and is permitted to do so. This contrasts with a non-NPDES permitted POTW, which may accept the same types of wastes as a permitted POTW but does not discharge the treated wastewater (such as, non-discharging lagoons that use evaporative techniques and/or land application).


This mapping application only includes NPDES permitted POTWs.


Public Water System (PWS)

A public water system provides water for human consumption through pipes or other constructed conveyances to at least 15 service connections or serves an average of at least 25 people for at least 60 days a year. A public water system may be publicly or privately owned. The three types of public water systems include: Community Water System (CWS), Non-Transient Non-Community Water System (NTNCWS), and Transient Non-Community Water System (TNCWS). This mapping application only includes Community Water Systems.


Service Area/Service Area Boundary

The area encompassing all service connections of a given Public Water System or Publicly Owned Treatment Works. See Drinking Water Service Areas and Wastewater Service Areas for detailed information.  

 

Utility

A term used interchangeably with “Public Water System”, “Community Water System”, and “NPDES POTW” to encompass both drinking water systems and wastewater facilities.

Infrastructure Types


Water ICAT includes water infrastructure types where there are high quality, nationally comprehensive data. Currently, these types include:


  1. Drinking Water: Community Water Systems (CWS) and
  2. Wastewater: National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permitted Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTWs).


The limiting factor in not including other infrastructure types (such as, stormwater systems**, private domestic wells, septic systems, and non-discharging wastewater facilities) is national data availability. As data availability improves, more water infrastructure types may be added to this tool.

 

NOTE: EPA is undergoing efforts to improve the accuracy of the wastewater data. As such, Water ICAT may include a few municipal separate storm sewer systems (MS4s) but does not contain a comprehensive dataset, so the tool should not be used to screen for potential water infrastructure needs at MS4 facilities.
